newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey signs more pay deals with unions.
newsitem.headline: Turkey signs more pay deals with unions.

text.p: Turkey's government signed pay accords with unions representing 162,000 state workers on Sunday and Monday, but some 250,000 in other strategic industries were holding out, rejecting a 38 percent pay rise offer.
Some unions said they would launch new action to press for bigger rises after next weekend, including blocking shipments at state oil and petrochemical plants.
"We, as the coalition government, are finalising the fastest collective bargaining talks in the past 15 years," Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan said on Monday.

"The agreement reached between the government and representatives of workers will eliminate the anomalies in workers' salaries," Erbakan said at a ceremony for the signing of a pay deal with the Islamist labour confederation Hak-Is.

Under the deal, some 20,000 workers from steel, machinery, forestry and farm sectors will receive a 38 percent rise for the six months to September in addition to a monthly increase of 13 million lira ($98.48) per month.
The government will later adopt a monthly sliding scale system under which salaries will be increased in line with inflation. Year-on-year inflation was 77 percent in March.
A similar deal was signed on Sunday between the government and several unions under Turk-Is, the largest union confederation representing 1.5 million workers.

State Minister Nevzat Ercan, who signed the deal with Turk-Is for 142,000 workers from the electrical, water, gas, paper, farm, forestry, health and news sectors, said he expected other unions to follow suit. "I hope other talks will also result in the same way," he said.

But some Turk-Is member unions, which stepped up industrial action last week rejecting the government offer of a 38 percent rise, said they would stage a stronger action after a religious festival this weekend at state oil and petrochemical plants, blocking shipments and holding marches.

"Our future action will be much stronger and the workers will not be responsible for the result if the refineries stop operation," said Bayram Yildirim, head of the influential Petrol-Is trade union, a Turk-Is affiliate.
His union represent workers from state refinery Tupras, petroleum marketer Petrol Ofisi, petrochemicals company Petkim, pipeline company Botas and exploration concern Turkish Petroleum (TPAO).
"If the large gap between workers and personnel with special contracts is not closed to reasonable levels, we will carry on with more intense action," he told Reuters.
"There are 250,000 such resisting workers represented by several unions under Turk-Is," Yildirim said.

He said his union would meet on April 25 with several other unions including Harb-Is of military workers and Liman-Is of power workers to decide on the course of action if talks with the government failed.
Turkey has banned industrial strikes in strategic sectors including oil and electricity, but workers of such industries usually stage go-slows by way of protest.
With the agreement signed on Sunday, Turk-Is has so far struck pay deals for some 160,000 workers from the total of 500,000 workers whose collective agreements ended at end-1996.
